key_terms.meaning: The agreed set of rules — syntax, semantics and timing — that two communicating devices follow so that the bits they exchange mean the same thing at both ends.
Both devices send and receive at the same time, like a phone call or a UPI payment while the app is still syncing.
Both devices can send, but only one at a time; the other waits its turn, as on a walkie-talkie.
A connection where more than two devices share the same link or medium, so the link capacity must be shared.
The physical path that carries the signal — twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fibre, or free-space radio.
Local area network: spans a room to a campus, is owned and run by one organisation, and offers high speed at low cost per port.
Wide area network: spans states or countries and runs over links leased from a telecom provider, so the organisation does not own the wire.
A private logical network built as tunnels across public Internet links, replacing an expensive private leased line at lower cost but with no bandwidth guarantee.
The geometric pattern in which links join nodes — bus, star, ring, mesh, tree or hybrid — which fixes the cable cost, port cost and fault tolerance.
Every node pair has its own link: most fault tolerant and needs no shared-access rules, but link count is n(n−1)/2 for n nodes, so it is costly.
Protocol data unit: the chunk of data at one layer, named differently per layer — bit, frame, packet, segment, message.
The part of a protocol that says what each field means and what action a receiver must take when it reads a given value.
A seven-layer model — physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application — that gives each networking job exactly one home.
Each layer takes the PDU from the layer above, puts its own header in front, and passes the whole thing down as its own data.
The design of the TCP/IP suite in which one protocol, IP, is the only common layer between many upper and many lower protocols, so new apps and new links plug in without redesign.
A fixed end-to-end path with reserved capacity is set up before data flows and released after; capacity is guaranteed but idle time is wasted.
A node receives the whole packet, checks it, and only then sends it on, so each hop costs one transmission time of delay.
The variation in packet delay from one packet to the next; it hurts real-time voice and video even when average delay is acceptable.
The set of devices whose transmissions can collide because they share one medium; a hub extends one, a switch ends it per port.
A switch or bridge sends a frame out of every port except the one it arrived on, used when the destination MAC address is not yet in the table.

takeaways: Data communication needs five parts — message, sender, receiver, medium and protocol — and a link can carry data simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex.
Networks are named by span and ownership: LAN is one organisation over a room-to-campus, MAN is a city run by a provider, WAN crosses states on provider links.
A topology is a cost-versus-fault-tolerance bargain; mesh buys reliability with n(n−1)/2 links, star buys cheap growth with a single point of failure at the centre.
A protocol is rules with syntax, semantics and timing, and without shared standards two correct machines still cannot talk.
Layering trades header overhead and some lost detail for modularity, easier teaching and testing, and the freedom to change one layer without touching the others.
OSI is a teaching and design reference; the real Internet runs TCP/IP, and its narrow waist at IP is what let the network grow so far.
Circuit switching reserves a path for the whole call; packet switching shares links store-and-forward, wasting less capacity but giving variable delay and jitter.
Devices map one-to-one onto layers: hub at physical, bridge and switch at data link, router at network — so the address a device reads tells you its layer.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask you to draw a layered diagram, name the PDU and address used at each layer, and then compare two designs — OSI versus TCP/IP, or circuit versus packet — on named criteria such as delay, overhead, cost and fault tolerance.

bank.q: List the five components of data communication and explain each with a small example.
outline: Message: the data being exchanged, text, numbers, image, audio or video.
Sender and receiver: the devices that originate and consume the message; each needs a protocol stack.
Medium: the physical path, twisted pair, coaxial, fibre or radio.
Protocol: the rules of syntax, semantics and timing that both ends obey.
Say clearly that a missing component means no communication, e.g. two machines with a cable but different protocols cannot exchange data.

bank.q: Distinguish simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex transmission, giving one real example of each.
outline: Simplex: one direction only, always; example keyboard to computer or a TV broadcast.
Half-duplex: both directions but one at a time; example walkie-talkie.
Full-duplex: both directions at once; example telephone call, or a link carrying data up and down together.
Connect the mode to capacity: full-duplex needs separate paths or echo cancellation and gives roughly twice the usable throughput.

bank.q: Compare LAN, MAN and WAN on span, ownership, speed and cost.
outline: LAN: room to campus, single organisation owns the equipment, high speed, low cost per port.
MAN: a city, usually a provider's links, moderate speed, higher cost.
WAN: across states or countries, on provider leased lines, lowest speed per rupee, highest cost.
Mention that the boundary is by ownership and span, not by technology, and that a VPN lets a WAN behave like a private network over the Internet.

bank.q: Explain the seven layers of the OSI reference model and give one job for each layer.
outline: Physical: bits onto the medium, voltages, connectors, data rate.
Data link: framing, error detection, MAC addressing, access control.
Network: logical addressing and routing of packets across networks.
Transport: end-to-end delivery, segmentation, reliability, flow control, ports.
Session: setting up and managing dialogue between applications.
Presentation: translation, compression, encryption.
Application: the user-facing service such as mail or web.
Name the PDU per layer and say the model is a reference, not a product.

bank.q: What are syntax, semantics and timing in a protocol? Why are standards needed?
outline: Syntax: format of the fields, their order and sizes.
Semantics: meaning of each field and the action to be taken.
Timing: when to send, how fast, and the order of exchange.
Standards let equipment from different vendors interoperate; bodies such as ISO, ITU-T, IEEE and IETF publish them, with RFCs for Internet protocols.
Two systems can be individually correct and still fail if they disagree on any of the three.

bank.q: Describe a hub, a bridge or switch, and a router, and state the layer and address each uses.
outline: Hub: physical layer, repeats bits to all ports, one collision domain, no address look-up.
Bridge or switch: data link layer, forwards frames by MAC address using a learn, forward, filter, flood table.
Router: network layer, forwards packets by IP address between different networks, and changes the link-layer frame at each hop.
Consequence: a switch keeps local traffic local, a router is needed to cross subnets.

bank.q: For n nodes, work out the number of links for a full mesh and for a star, and compare with a bus. Which do you choose for a 40-seat lab and why?
outline: Full mesh: n(n−1)/2 duplex links, and each node needs n−1 ports.
Star: n links and n+1 ports if there is a central device.
Bus: one backbone cable with taps, cheapest but one break or one bad tap kills the network.
For a 40-seat lab: star, because cable and port count grow linearly and one faulty cable removes only one node.
State the trade-off: mesh gives fault tolerance and no shared-access problem at high cost; star gives cheap growth with a central single point of failure.

bank.q: Trace one HTTP request from a browser to the bits on the wire. Name the PDU and the address used at each layer.
outline: Application: an HTTP message, using a host name resolved to an IP address.
Transport: TCP segment, with source and destination port numbers.
Network: IP packet, with source and destination IP addresses, routed hop by hop.
Data link: frame with source and destination MAC addresses, valid only for the current hop.
Physical: bits as signal on the medium.
At each step the layer adds a header; at the receiver each header is stripped in reverse order.
Note that the MAC address changes every hop while the IP address stays the same end to end.

bank.q: A link of R bits per second carries packets of L bits over a path of N links, ignoring propagation and queueing. Derive the store-and-forward delay for one packet and for P packets.
outline: One hop transmission time is L/R seconds.
One packet over N links with store-and-forward is N × L/R, since each router must receive the whole packet before sending it.
For P packets the last packet finishes at time (N + P − 1) × L/R.
Define every symbol and state the units in seconds.
Mention the simplifying assumptions: no propagation, no queueing, no processing delay.

bank.q: A circuit-switched link of 1 Mbps is divided into 100 kbps circuits. How many users fit? What changes if packet switching is used and each user is active only 10 percent of the time?
outline: Circuit switching supports 1 Mbps ÷ 100 kbps = 10 simultaneous users.
The eleventh user is blocked even if the other ten are idle, so capacity is wasted.
With packet switching users share the full 1 Mbps on demand and can exceed 10, at the risk of queueing delay.
Quote the usual result: the number of users that can be supported with small probability of congestion is several times 10.
Conclude that packet switching suits bursty data, circuit switching suits steady streams.

bank.q: A frame with destination MAC address not in the switch table arrives at a switch port. Describe step by step what the switch does.
outline: Learn: record source MAC address with the incoming port and a timestamp.
Look up the destination MAC address in the table.
No entry found, so flood: send out all ports except the incoming one.
The reply from the destination lets the switch learn that address too.
If the entry exists, forward on the matching port; if the entry is on the incoming port itself, filter and drop.
Entries age out so that a moved device is relearned.

bank.q: Compare circuit switching and packet switching on setup delay, utilisation, end-to-end delay and jitter. Recommend one for live voice and one for file download, with reasons.
outline: Circuit switching: setup and teardown phases, reserved capacity, constant delay, near-zero jitter, but idle capacity is wasted.
Packet switching: no setup, statistical sharing, better utilisation, but variable queueing delay and jitter, and possible loss.
Datagram versus virtual circuit: the second keeps a per-flow path but still shares links.
Voice: small constant rate, delay sensitive, so circuit switching or a packet network with reservation and priority.
File download: bursty, delay tolerant, so packet switching is far more efficient.

bank.q: Discuss the advantages and drawbacks of layering. Why does layering sometimes duplicate functions and lose detail?
outline: Advantages: modularity, one job per layer, easier teaching and testing, independent replacement of a layer, standard interfaces between vendors.

Drawbacks: header overhead at every layer, processing cost, and information hiding that hides useful detail — for example error checks repeated at several layers because a lower layer cannot assume the upper ones are present.
Lost detail: a layer cannot see parameters it might exploit, such as wireless loss at the transport layer.
Duplicated function: error control and flow control appear at more than one layer.
Conclude that layering is a design bargain, not a law, and cross-layer designs trade modularity for performance.

bank.q: Compare the OSI reference model with the TCP/IP protocol suite. Why did TCP/IP become the working standard?
outline: OSI: seven layers, a clean reference with separate session and presentation layers, produced as a standard before a working implementation.
TCP/IP: four layers — application, transport, internet, network access — with session and presentation folded into the application, and a proven implementation first.
TCP/IP has a narrow waist at IP, letting new link technologies below and new applications above plug in.
Simplicity and free, open RFC specifications encouraged wide adoption.
OSI is still valuable vocabulary for teaching and for reasoning about which layer a fault is in.

bank.q: Design the network for a two-building campus of 300 users with a server room. Choose topologies, devices and links, and justify the choices against cost and fault tolerance.
outline: Access layer: star topology per floor with switches, so one cable fault affects one seat.
Backbone: a fibre link between the two buildings and to the server room, possibly a redundant second path.
Distribution: routers or layer-3 switches to separate subnets per department and control broadcast traffic.
Devices by layer: hubs are avoided because they extend one collision domain; switches forward by MAC inside a subnet, routers forward by IP between subnets.
Fault tolerance versus cost: a full mesh backbone is unnecessary; a redundant ring or dual-homed core is a reasonable compromise.
Mention that a provider WAN link or VPN is needed only for outside access, not inside the campus.

glossary.def: The exchange of data between two devices through a message, a sender, a receiver, a medium and a common protocol.
A transmission mode in which data flows in one direction only, always.
A connection that links exactly two devices, so the whole link capacity belongs to that pair.
Personal area network: a very short-range network around one person, such as Bluetooth between a phone and earbuds.
The part of a network that connects end hosts to the first provider or campus router.
The inner part of a network made of high-capacity links and routers that carry aggregated traffic between access networks.
Two or more networks joined by routers so that hosts on different networks can exchange data.
All nodes tap one shared backbone cable, cheapest to wire but with one shared collision domain and a single cable as a failure point.
Every node has its own link to a central device, so growth is cheap and one cable fault isolates one node, but the centre is a single point of failure.
Each node connects to two neighbours forming a closed loop, giving a predictable path and possible dual-ring recovery at the cost of break handling.
The part of a protocol that fixes the layout, order and size of fields in a message.
The part of a protocol that states when data may be sent, at what rate, and in what order.
A level in a layered architecture that performs one group of related jobs and offers a defined service to the layer above.
The same layer on the other machine, which reads the header that its own layer added at the sender.
The extra bytes each layer adds to the data, which reduce the fraction of each transmission that is useful payload.
The data link layer PDU, carrying MAC addresses and a trailer for error detection.
The network layer PDU, carrying source and destination IP addresses so routers can forward it.
The transport layer PDU in TCP, carrying port numbers and sequence information.
The defined boundary through which one layer passes data and parameters to the layer directly below it.
The four-layer protocol stack — application, transport, internet, network access — on which the Internet runs.
An end device that runs applications and sends or receives traffic, as opposed to a router that forwards others' traffic.
A packet that carries its full destination address and is forwarded independently, with no prior path set up.
A packet-switched flow that follows a path set up in advance and is identified by a short label rather than a full address.
A data link layer device that forwards frames by MAC address and gives each port its own collision domain.
A network layer device that forwards packets between different networks by looking up the destination IP address.
The International Organization for Standardization, the body that published the OSI reference model.
The Internet Engineering Task Force, the open body that develops Internet standards and publishes them as RFCs.
